Definition: Whether a detailed implementation roadmap with phases, milestones, and timelines exists for data exchange development
Comments: The National Telecommunications and Informatics Strategy 2023-2027 exists (GIA referenced it for root server deployment). However, a detailed data exchange implementation roadmap with phases and milestones is not confirmed as publicly available.
revision_notes: Original sources (Libya Herald root-server launch article; TU Delft e-government paper) were fetched and confirmed relevant but only established the existence of the 2023-2027 Telecommunications and Informatics Strategy, not a detailed data exchange roadmap. Targeted search found a GIA-hosted UN-ESCWA report, 'Interoperability Frameworks: Best Practices and Roadmap' (dated December 2025, published on gia.gov.ly), which sets out a detailed four-phase proposed roadmap (Preparation, Design, Implementation, Sustainability) with indicative timelines for building the Libyan Government Interoperability Framework (LyGIF), plus confirmation that the PM approved a National Strategy for Government Digital Transformation in April 2025. This is materially stronger and fresher evidence, but the interoperability roadmap is explicitly framed as a proposed action plan from an ESCWA consultancy report rather than a formally adopted government roadmap with binding milestones. Value Code confirmed at 2 (Under development) on the strength of this fresher evidence rather than upgraded to 'Yes', since formal adoption is not yet confirmed.
revised_comments: Libya's General Information Authority (GIA), working with UN-ESCWA, has published a detailed report titled 'Interoperability Frameworks: Best Practices and Roadmap' (December 2025) that proposes a four-phase implementation roadmap - preparation, design, implementation and sustainability - for building the Libyan Government Interoperability Framework (LyGIF), including indicative phase timelines such as a six-to-nine month implementation stage. This complements the National Strategy for Government Digital Transformation approved by the Prime Minister in April 2025, whose implementation has reportedly begun in several ministries. The interoperability roadmap remains a proposed action plan rather than a formally adopted government roadmap with binding milestones, placing data exchange implementation planning at an under-development stage.

Definition: Whether a formal strategy or policy document exists specifically for government data exchange and interoperability
Comments: The National Committee for Digital Transformation was established in 2022 and is developing a digital strategy with a target for implementation by 2030. The GIA's remit includes digital transformation strategy. References to 'national interoperability framework' and 'cross-government architecture' appear in academic analysis and policy discourse, but a formally adopted comprehensive strategy document is not yet confirmed publicly.
revision_notes: Original sources (TU Delft e-government paper; Shwehdy commentary on fragmented digital governance) were fetched and confirmed relevant but reflected an earlier stage where only a 2022 committee and broader academic discourse existed. Targeted search found that Libya's Prime Minister formally approved a National Strategy for Government Digital Transformation in April 2025 (a broader digital strategy, GIA-sourced), and that a strategy process specific to data exchange and interoperability is now under active development: the GIA/UN-ESCWA 'Interoperability Frameworks: Best Practices and Roadmap' report (December 2025) proposing the Libyan Government Interoperability Framework (LyGIF), and a proposed National Cloud Computing Policy for government data (January 2026, GIA/ESCWA). Together these show a dedicated data exchange/interoperability strategy process is now under development, beyond being merely mentioned within a broader strategy. Value Code revised from 2 (mentioned in broader strategy) to 3 (under development).
revised_comments: Libya's Prime Minister approved a National Strategy for Government Digital Transformation in April 2025, covering four tracks - an integrated digital government, a competitive digital economy, an inclusive digital society and a safe digital environment - with implementation reportedly underway in several ministries. Specifically for data exchange and interoperability, the General Information Authority is developing the Libyan Government Interoperability Framework (LyGIF) with UN-ESCWA support, evidenced by a detailed best-practice and roadmap report (December 2025) and a proposed National Cloud Computing Policy (January 2026) covering government data hosting and sovereignty. These interoperability-specific instruments are under active development but have not yet been formally adopted as a standalone, comprehensive strategy document.

Definition: Provisions ensuring national control over government data and protecting against unauthorized foreign access
Comments: Libya enacted Law No. 6/2022 on Electronic Transactions including data protection provisions, and Law No. 5/2022 on Combating Cybercrime. The National Telecommunications and Informatics Strategy 2023-2027 references digital sovereignty. Root servers were launched in 2025 to enhance digital sovereignty. However, the legal framework remains partially implemented and no standalone data protection authority exists.
revision_notes: Original sources (dig.watch on Law 6/2022; Libya Herald on root servers; DLA Piper data protection guide) were fetched and confirmed accurate but reflected an earlier, more limited picture of 'partially implemented' controls. Fresh search found that the Central Bank of Libya issued a Personal Data Protection Regulation (Circular No. 18, June 2025) imposing a mandatory, penalty-backed prohibition on storing personal, financial or credit data outside Libya for all CBL-regulated entities (banks, fintechs, payment providers), binding from 1 July 2026, with the regulator explicitly rejecting exceptions for cloud storage or encrypted backups abroad. This sits alongside confirmation that Libya's root servers became operational in Tripoli and Benghazi in October 2025 (reducing dependence on foreign internet infrastructure) and that a National Cloud Computing Policy for government data hosting and sovereignty is under development with UN-ESCWA support (January 2026). This is materially stronger evidence of enforceable controls than 'limited controls', though it remains sector-specific (financial services) rather than a comprehensive, government-wide data sovereignty regime, and no dedicated general data protection authority exists. Value Code revised from 2 (limited controls) to 3 (strong yet unenforced/not-yet-comprehensive controls).
revised_comments: Libya has a growing body of legal and technical measures supporting data sovereignty. Law No. 6/2022 on Electronic Transactions and Law No. 5/2022 on Combating Cybercrime provide a legal basis for data protection and establish the National Authority for Information Security and Safety (NISSA) to oversee electronic authentication and ICT security. The Central Bank of Libya's Personal Data Protection Regulation (Circular No. 18, June 2025) imposes a mandatory, penalty-backed prohibition on storing personal, financial or credit data outside Libya for all CBL-regulated financial entities, binding from July 2026. Libya's root name servers went live in Tripoli and Benghazi in October 2025, reducing dependence on foreign internet infrastructure, and a National Cloud Computing Policy for government data hosting is under development with UN-ESCWA support (January 2026). These provisions are substantive and increasingly enforceable but remain sector-specific (financial services) or still at proposal stage for government data generally, and no dedicated general data protection authority with government-wide oversight yet exists.
